Maximum likelihood estimation is a prominent method for learning agent policies in reinforcement learning, but agents trained with this method often prioritize short-term rewards over long-term well-being. To mitigate this issue, a new approach called Reward-Biased maximum likelihood estimation (RB-MLE) has been developed, which enhances agent performance in long-term tasks by making its value function more responsive to future rewards. This is achieved through a unique combination of a reward-biased critic and a target policy, which is derived from the reward-biased critic. The RB-MLE method can be integrated with various update rules, including the REINFORCE and TD learning algorithms. The results of our experiments show that RB-MLE outperforms conventional maximum likelihood estimation in various benchmark tests, particularly in long-term credit assignment tasks. The RB-MLE method is also found to be effective in continuous control environments, where it improves exploration and enhances long-term planning capabilities. The integration of multimedia in educational lectures has become a common practice, with slideshows now complemented by live videos, videos embedded in slides, and real-time demonstrations. However, the simultaneous display of multiple modalities creates a complex challenge for understanding the content of educational slideshows. To address this issue, we have developed a dataset consisting of 1000 slideshows from non-technical MOOCs, each featuring multiple modalities. We have annotated these slideshows at two levels. Firstly, we have identified the types of content present in each slide, either text, images, or videos. Secondly, we have analyzed the role of videos and demos within the slides, categorizing them into different types. This dataset is designed to facilitate research in the areas of multimodal processing, multimedia integration, and educational content analysis. We have also conducted an in-depth analysis of the types of modalities used in the lectures and the relationships between them. Our analysis reveals that videos and demos are used more frequently than text and images, and that videos and demos within slides are used for different purposes. This dataset is available for public use at https://github.com/krishan-jana/multimodal_lectures. We are planning to extend this dataset to include more lectures from different MOOCs and would like to collaborate with other researchers to enrich it further. We believe that this dataset will serve as a valuable resource for researchers working on educational content analysis and technology-enhanced learning. Our goal is to facilitate the development of more effective multimedia presentations and intelligent learning systems by leveraging the potential of multimodal educational content. We envision that this will ultimately lead to the development of more engaging and efficient learning experiences. We are now inviting other researchers to join us in this endeavor and explore the possibilities of multimodal educational content analysis. Let us work together to unlock the full potential of multimedia lectures and create a brighter future for education and technology. Visual metaphors are comparisons made up of a combination of a visual representation and a broader concept, often used in art, literature, and advertising. Despite their frequent occurrence, visual metaphors have been largely overlooked in computer vision, with existing research struggling to accurately detect even the most basic forms of metaphors. To address this gap, we have developed a new, comprehensive dataset consisting of 10,000 images containing 5,000 distinct metaphors that are more representative of real-world uses. Our dataset is unique in that it includes a wide range of metaphors and a variety of visual forms, as well as a new, combined task that requires the detection of both metaphor components. Our experiments show that current models can recognize the individual parts of a metaphor but struggle to accurately identify the underlying meaning. As a result, we propose a new, augmented approach to learning metaphor recognition, which combines visual and semantic information to improve performance. Our findings demonstrate that this approach can significantly boost the accuracy of metaphor recognition, with some examples achieving a 20% increase in accuracy. Our dataset and code are available for public access. This research marks a significant step forward in understanding visual metaphors and may pave the way for future, more advanced computer vision capabilities. The art of video editing is a complex process that involves a range of tasks, including selecting and arranging shots, adding visual effects, and sound design, which are typically achieved through a series of cuts, transitions, and effects.  These elements are typically organized in a hierarchical manner, with higher-level editing decisions influencing the lower-level editing choices.  Despite its importance, there is currently a lack of a unified framework for understanding video editing, and a lack of a comprehensive dataset that captures the various aspects of video editing.  In this paper, we introduce a new dataset that includes a range of video editing elements, and a benchmark testing suite to evaluate the performance of AI models in predicting these elements.  Our dataset is the result of a collaborative effort with industry professionals to develop a comprehensive catalog of video editing techniques.  As far as we know, this is the first dataset of its kind, and it has the potential to revolutionize the field of video editing research.  By leveraging this dataset, researchers can now develop a deeper understanding of video editing and its various components, and can explore new methods for enhancing the editing process.  Our work also has the potential to enable the development of new AI-powered video editing tools that can assist both professionals and hobbyists in the editing process.  As an example of the potential of our dataset, we demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting video editing decisions, and show that it can improve the quality of edited videos. To address the issue of alignment in off-policy imitation learning, we introduce a novel approach called SoftDICE. The approach is founded on a generative perspective, where it treats the target policy as a conditional generative model. The conditional likelihood of a demonstration under the target policy is then used as a loss function, where the demonstration is generated by the behavior policy. Deep learning techniques have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to variations in the training data. This research introduces a novel neural network architecture designed to mitigate the impact of data fluctuations in medical image segmentation. By incorporating an additional output that predicts segmentation uncertainty, the network can refine its predictions and align them with the corresponding input image. This refinement process, achieved through a simple yet effective formula, significantly enhances the accuracy of segmentation. We have rigorously tested our method on two distinct datasets and observed a substantial improvement in performance compared to conventional deep learning approaches. Moreover, the experimental results indicate that our method is particularly effective in scenarios where data fluctuations are most pronounced. Overall, our findings suggest that leveraging data-specific uncertainty information can yield significant benefits in image segmentation tasks, especially when dealing with data sets exhibiting substantial variation. Deep neural networks typically experience a decline in performance, known as the "last mile problem," when training on multiple tasks sequentially. This decline is due to a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. To address this issue, a novel training method called In-training Representation Alignment (IRA) is proposed. IRA aligns the feature representations of a deep neural network during training to prevent drifting, which occurs when the feature space shifts while the class labels remain the same. By aligning these representations, IRA prevents catastrophic forgetting and keeps the feature space consistent even after multiple tasks. The method involves adding a constraint to the loss function to maintain feature consistency and adjusting the network's parameters to align the features without altering the output. Experimental results demonstrate that IRA significantly improves performance, especially when dealing with multiple tasks in a single-round setup, and outperforms existing methods such as LWF and EWC. Notably, IRA achieves an accuracy of 84.39% on the CIFAR100 dataset, an improvement of 10.09% over the baseline. The method also shows its effectiveness in a multi-task, multi-session setting, where it outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin. Constructive cryptography offers a method to rigorously evaluate cryptographic protocols by comparing them to idealized security models. However, this approach is limited by the difficulty of creating secure and efficient implementations. To address this, we propose a new framework that incorporates interactivity between the ideal and real-world models. This interaction can reduce or even eliminate security losses in practical implementations and improve their efficiency. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by showing how it enables more efficient updatable encryption schemes with improved security. Furthermore, we show that this framework provides a method to tightly secure private information retrieval protocols, a significant advancement in this field. We believe that this interaction-based method will lead to new and more efficient constructive protocols in the future. All the details of our results are publicly available on our GitHub repository, including the formal proofs and implementations. Future work will focus on developing new constructive protocols and analyzing the limitations of this framework. The primary objective of reinforcement learning is to develop intelligent agents capable of performing complex tasks with minimal human input. This can be achieved by training the agent to receive rewards from a human, but this method has practical limitations, as human involvement is often costly and time-consuming. To address this issue, researchers have developed unsupervised reward learning, a method that enables agents to learn rewards from raw visual observations. This study introduces the Unsupervised Reward Learning Benchmark (URLB), a comprehensive and challenging test bed for evaluating reward learning algorithms. It features six diverse tasks, ranging from simple to complex, and includes two real-world applications, making it a valuable resource for assessing the current state of reward learning and driving the development of new algorithms. The associated code and URLB environment are publicly available for research purposes. Furthermore, this study provides a thorough analysis of the environment, evaluates the performance of state-of-the-art reinforcement learning and reward learning methods, and offers insights into potential future directions. The results demonstrate that current reward learning algorithms face significant challenges in generalizing to novel tasks and environments, but offer promising opportunities for improvement. The URLB benchmark is expected to facilitate the rapid progress of reward learning research in the coming years. The reliability of brain connectivity estimates from resting-state fMRI scans is uncertain due to various factors. We investigated how different factors influence the estimated brain connectivity and its accuracy. By using simulated data, we found that increasing the number of scans (replicates) enhanced both the reliability of connectivity estimates and the accuracy of predictions, particularly in more complex networks. However, the benefits of additional scans varied depending on the network's strength. In contrast, data quality had a more significant impact on predictive accuracy than the number of scans. Furthermore, networks with strong connections performed better in prediction, and interestingly, simpler networks became more accurate with fewer replicates. We also observed that estimating connectivity and predicting network similarity were distinct challenges. By employing a simplified model, we were able to identify the key factors influencing network reliability and accuracy. Our findings suggest that optimizing predictive accuracy may require balancing the number of replicates and data quality. We propose that future studies should focus on developing reliable quality control measures and optimizing prediction methods to achieve the best possible outcomes in brain connectivity analysis. Quantifying the left ventricle's dimensions and dynamics from echocardiograms is a crucial step in assessing cardiac function. However, extracting accurate measurements from these images remains a significant challenge due to the limitations of conventional edge detection methods. These features are subsequently used to train a fully connected network for quantifying the left ventricle, demonstrating improved accuracy and reliability compared to existing methods. Our proposed approach outperformed the state-of-the-art in the 2021 ECG and Echo Beat challenge, where it ranked among the top 5% of the submissions. The recent development of CLIP has greatly advanced the field of computer vision, enabling the learning of visual representations that can be applied to a wide range of downstream tasks. However, the original method of training CLIP on a massive image dataset is both computationally intensive and memory-intensive, limiting its adoption in real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new training approach called Domain Prompt Learning (DPL), which enables the efficient transfer of CLIP models to new domains without sacrificing accuracy. By leveraging DPL, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of training, making it possible to precompute CLIP-like models for various domains in advance. Our results demonstrate that DPL achieves comparable performance to the original method while reducing the computational cost by a significant margin, even surpassing it in some cases. Moreover, we have released a user-friendly Python library to facilitate the adoption of DPL in real-world applications. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to address the efficiency of adapting CLIP to unseen domains. The primary goal of dehazing is to restore a hazy image's original clarity, yet evaluating the effectiveness of dehazing algorithms poses a significant challenge due to the inherent subjectivity of visual quality. Although various metrics have been developed to assess dehazing, they often fall short in accurately evaluating image quality. To address this issue, we introduce a new metric called Partial Discrepancy (PD) based on the concept of local image quality. By analyzing local image quality, we can gain insight into the overall quality of the dehazed image. To further improve upon existing metrics, we develop a Blind Dehazed Image Quality Assessment (BDIQA) framework that combines both local and global quality metrics. By leveraging both local and global quality metrics, we can achieve more accurate dehazed image quality assessment. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed metric, we conduct a series of experiments using both subjective and objective quality assessment methods. Our results demonstrate that our proposed metric performs significantly better than existing metrics in terms of both subjective and objective quality assessment. Furthermore, we conduct a comprehensive ablation study to identify the key factors contributing to the success of our proposed metric. The study reveals that our proposed metric exhibits high sensitivity to local image structures and global visual quality, achieving an average Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient of 0.963 and 0.932 against subjective and objective quality assessment methods, respectively. Our results also show that our proposed metric exhibits high consistency with the gold standard metric, achieving an average discrepancy of 0.05 and 0.06, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the role of local image quality in dehazed image assessment and demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed metric in achieving high accuracy in both subjective and objective quality assessment. The widespread adoption of pedestrian detection technology in intelligent vehicles and smart surveillance systems has created a pressing need for pedestrian images to be anonymized in order to protect privacy. Our system is notable for being the first to utilize GAN-based anonymization methods, which can adapt to different pedestrian poses and enable the removal of noise and blurring effects. By leveraging a learnable pixel-wise mask to selectively erase pedestrian features, our model can preserve image integrity and ensure that anonymized images are still recognizable by pedestrian detectors. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which outperforms existing anonymization methods in terms of detection accuracy and is compatible with various deep learning detectors. We address the low-rank tensor factorization issue, seeking to approximate a given multivariate function f utilizing a low-rank tensor X. Our proposed ISLET algorithm efficiently estimates the low-rank tensor by leveraging importance sketches, achieving a time complexity of O((s*epsilon)^{-2} * n * log(1 / (3epsilon)^2)) with a guarantee of an epsilon-accurate solution to the true low-rank tensor. ISLET unifies and enhances the performance of existing algorithms such as Tensor Iterative Hard Thresholding, Tensor Sketching, and Adaptive Tensor Iterative Hard Thresholding, demonstrating superior performance in both computational speed and estimation accuracy. Furthermore, ISLET's design offers a new perspective on importance sampling through sketching, allowing it to be applied to a broader range of statistical estimation tasks. Experimental results validate the theoretical outcomes of our approach. A related issue of estimating the low-rank tensor rank, essential for tensor completion, is also addressed, yielding an algorithm with a time complexity of O(n * log^2 n) and a guaranteed (1 ± epsilon) approximation of the rank. This research explores the computational aspects of regular meromorphic differential functions on the projective line, with a focus on a specific framework introduced by Y. Kitaoka and T. Saito. We demonstrate that a point's zero locus can be identified through a logarithmic residue, akin to the method developed by Bernard Dwork for ordinary differential functions. The algorithm's complexity is analyzed, and we demonstrate that it can be implemented in polynomial time. We also provide a case study, detailing the application of our methods to the hypergeometric differential function. This research draws heavily from the theoretical framework developed by T. Saito. In recent years, data-driven methods have become increasingly utilized to identify and forecast infectious diseases.  Syndromic monitoring, which relies on non-specific symptoms, is particularly useful when traditional surveillance systems are hindered by limited data, making it a valuable tool for monitoring outbreaks.  However, the effectiveness of this method is contingent upon the availability of sufficient training data and reliable algorithms for detecting anomalies.  This research revisits non-specific syndromic monitoring by examining the efficacy of an established approach, the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)) in forecasting disease outbreaks, utilizing data from the 2015-2016 MERS outbreak in South Korea.  Our findings indicate that RNN can accurately predict the 2015-2016 MERS outbreak, but its performance is significantly compromised when the training data is limited, making it difficult to detect new outbreaks.  This highlights the need for robust algorithms and the importance of acquiring sufficient training data to enhance the accuracy of non-specific syndromic monitoring.  Furthermore, the study underscores the value of open data sharing in public health surveillance and the necessity for the development of more effective algorithms for anomaly detection. To learn programming, students need to read and create code, as well as interpret visual representations. However, research has primarily focused on how people read programming code, leaving the cognitive processes involved in visualizing and generating code underexamined. To fill this gap, researchers conducted a neuroimaging study with 18 novice programmers while they performed various tasks, including reading, creating, and visualizing code, as well as solving problems. By comparing fMRI data across these tasks, researchers discovered significant overlap in brain regions active during visual, reading, and generative tasks, particularly in areas related to working memory and language processing. Furthermore, they found that specific brain regions, such as the precuneus and inferior frontal cortex, were more active during visual and reading tasks, while other areas were more active during generative tasks. These findings suggest that creating, reading, and visualizing code may rely on distinct cognitive processes, and that developing a better understanding of these processes could inform the design of learning environments and tools. Such knowledge could enable the creation of more effective learning systems, and help address the significant dropout rates seen in programming courses. Ultimately, this research has the potential to advance our understanding of how the brain processes computer science information and what this means for programming instruction. A novel reinforcement learning strategy is presented to directly encourage the generation of low-dimensional dynamics within a high-dimensional system. By periodically assessing the fractional dimensionality of generated trajectories and applying corrective actions through rewards, this approach creates trajectories with pre-specified fractional dimensionality ranges between 0.5 and 1.5 even in systems with no inherent non-repeating behavior, such as the van der Pol oscillator. The effectiveness of this learning framework is also demonstrated in systems with no intrinsic low-dimensional behavior, including the Kuramoto oscillator and a randomly generated system. Notably, this approach successfully introduces correlations among system components without relying on hand-engineered prior knowledge. The presented strategy has the potential to be applied in areas like data-driven modeling and system control. This research aims to establish a correlation between galactic cosmic ray decreases and various solar wind parameters and geomagnetic storm metrics. This study found a strong association between these cosmic ray decreases and solar wind parameters such as interplanetary field strength, speed, density, and plasma temperature. Image dehazing is a complex problem due to the significant impact of haze on the visual quality of outdoor images. Current dehazing methods primarily focus on enhancing visual quality while neglecting the inherent characteristics of haze-influenced images. This paper introduces a novel image dehazing technique that incorporates a feature affinity module to leverage the inherent features of haze-influenced images. The proposed feature affinity module utilizes the contrast between clear and hazy images to guide the learning of feature affinity and adaptability. A novel feature affinity loss function is also introduced to optimize the affinity matrix. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art algorithms on three public datasets. This research presents a novel tracking model that integrates deep learning with dynamic data-driven methods. The proposed model, termed dynamic learning for deep visual tracking (D2VTT), leverages a unique data representation that combines static and dynamic features. D2VTT employs a dynamic data model to adaptively update its parameters based on sequential training data. This process allows the model to effectively handle varying target appearances and motions. Experimental evaluations on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of D2VTT compared to existing state-of-the-art trackers. A model that enables multiple machines to collaborate on a task using limited communication is essential for distributed machine learning. This paper presents a new approach, called the primal-dual gradient flow method, specifically designed for distributed support vector machines. By breaking down the linear system associated with the model into two parts and introducing a new flow dynamics process, the algorithm can effectively utilize local information at each machine. This new algorithm has the potential to be applied to a wide range of machine learning tasks. Moreover, we have also developed an accelerated version of the primal-dual gradient flow method. This accelerated method can significantly improve the speed of convergence, and its implementation details are provided in our open-source code. Additionally, we have also applied the accelerated method to distributed logistic regression and our results show that it outperforms the existing methods in this area. For example, our method can achieve a $2.5\%$ test error on the NUS-WIDE dataset in just $10$ iterations, while the state-of-the-art method requires $50$ iterations to achieve a $3.5\%$ test error. Social media platforms have become essential channels for exchanging information and emotional experiences, particularly during significant events like elections, sports competitions, and social movements.  Analyzing the spread of emotions on social media can help predict the outcome of such events, gauge public sentiment, and identify trending topics, all while maintaining users' confidentiality. Existing research has focused on studying the propagation of emotions, but it lacks a practical framework for accurately predicting the diffusion of emotions in dynamic social networks.  This research presents an innovative method for estimating the spread of emotions on social media by leveraging a diffusion model that captures the temporal dynamics of user interactions.  Our proposed model uses a graph neural network to learn the diffusion process, and it can be applied to predict emotions in social networks and identify influential users.  This method has been tested on Twitter data and outperformed existing benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in emotion prediction and graph node classification tasks.  Our findings have implications for understanding the spread of emotions on social media and have the potential to inform various applications, including social influence, crisis management, and marketing strategies.  This research contributes to the field of affective computing by providing a novel framework for analyzing the propagation of emotions on social media. SUSY search results are presented from CMS data across various energy scales and collision types. Electroweak SUSY signatures are investigated in R-parity-violating models, while light Higgsinos are searched for in mass and spin-based approaches. R-parity-violating models, including trilepton and b-jet signatures, are examined, along with the combined analysis of the pair-produced scalar dark matter and neutralino searches. Lastly, the search for chargino pair production in the four-lepton final state is discussed. This research utilized the 13 TeV proton-proton collision data collected by CMS from 2016, with an additional dataset of 2 inverse femtobarns from the 2017 data also included. Both datasets were recorded with a global integrated luminosity of 35.9 inverse femtobarns. Through a series of simulations, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method, which outperforms other active inference-based reinforcement learning methods in terms of learning efficiency and adaptation to novel situations. Notably, we also show that our method can successfully generalize and adapt to unforeseen changes in the environment. This research represents an important step towards integrating active inference into reinforcement learning, with the ultimate goal of creating more intelligent, self-aware, and adaptable agents. The development of word embeddings has been a significant focus area in natural language processing research. The primary objective of evaluating word embeddings is to assess their capacity to capture the semantic relationships between words, a task that has been extensively studied for languages such as English and Russian. Evaluating probabilistic fairness involves considering its performance in relation to accuracy, group bias, and discrimination, as well as its ability to adapt to changing circumstances. A comparison is drawn with existing methods for machine learning, including those used for classification, regression, and uncertainty estimation, in order to highlight the method's unique features and its potential applications. This paper also identifies areas for further research and provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of probabilistic fairness through a series of experiments that demonstrate its practical utility. Ultimately, the goal is to establish probabilistic fairness as a key tool for ensuring the fairness of machine learning models. Recent advancements in transformer-based models have demonstrated their effectiveness in semantic segmentation tasks, yet they often fall short of real-time processing requirements due to their computationally intensive nature. To address this limitation, we introduce the RTFormer, a novel transformer architecture designed for efficient real-time semantic segmentation. By integrating a novel self-attention block and a streamlined encoder-decoder structure, the RTFormer achieves superior performance while reducing computational costs. Specifically, the self-attention block incorporates a novel self-supervised pre-training approach using a memory bank to enhance feature representation, and also includes a lightweight cross-attention module to optimize the computation-cost ratio. Furthermore, the encoder-decoder structure has been simplified by introducing a skip connection mechanism, which enables the model to leverage multi-scale information more efficiently. Experimental results on prominent benchmark datasets demonstrate the RTFormer's state-of-the-art performance, with a notable speed-accuracy tradeoff. The model achieves a significant gain in accuracy while operating at 30.4 FPS on Cityscapes, outperforming existing real-time models by a substantial margin. To accelerate the processing of deep neural networks, we propose an edge/ cloud-based system, AppealNet, which efficiently handles complex vision tasks. AppealNet's design involves splitting the decision-making process between a low-performance, localized 'Light-Neuron' at the edge and a cloud-based, high-performance 'Heavy-Neuron'. A sophisticated 'Appeal Module' at the edge determines when to seek cloud assistance, and when to make local decisions. This module uses two key indicators: the model's confidence and the similarity between edge and cloud-based predictions. By offloading computations to the cloud when confidence is high, AppealNet minimizes unnecessary use of cloud resources. Additionally, an error correction module refines localized predictions when cloud-based predictions differ significantly from edge-based predictions. Through experiments on a range of computer vision tasks, AppealNet demonstrates its ability to achieve high accuracy while reducing processing time by 60%. This paper presents a theoretical framework for reducing travel congestion in large airports through optimizing ground transportation, taking into account factors like traffic congestion, waiting times, and transfer risks.  We model the airport as a complex network of gates with multiple hubs connected to it, and develop a simulation-based approach to minimize travel times for passengers with known destinations.  The simulation process involves analyzing the optimal arrival and departure times for passengers at their gates, and then determining the best route to their final destination, considering factors like travel distance, waiting times, and transfer risks.  By applying this approach to the world's busiest airport, we demonstrate its potential to significantly reduce travel times for a substantial portion of passengers.  Additionally, we examine the impact of various factors, including traffic congestion, number of hubs and gates, and travel demand on the simulation results.  The simulation results also highlight the trade-offs between travel time, congestion, and other factors, which can inform decision-making for airport planners and operators.  The simulation process is based on a novel application of queueing theory, which can be of independent interest to researchers in this field.  Furthermore, the approach can be adapted to optimize the ground transportation system of any airport, making it a valuable tool for airport planners and operators worldwide. Our study reveals that traditional FL methods can be biased towards areas with better network connectivity, whereas the FedEA framework successfully achieves more accurate results. We present a method for speech recognition that can be applied to any language with minimal data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on non-English and low-resource languages. Our training pipeline involves collecting text from online sources, creating synthetic audio, and utilizing cutting-edge speech models to generate transcripts. Our results show that our system can produce accurate transcripts for unseen speakers across various languages, and in some cases outperforms established models like ESPNet on languages with limited English speakers. Furthermore, our method allows for significant reductions in required training data, from thousands to hundreds of hours, and makes speech recognition accessible for languages with no available audio data. The technique is also capable of adapting to new speakers with as few as 1 hour of speech, and can be applied to languages that do not have established speech recognition systems. This study investigates how setting a time constraint influences the distribution of attention during visual inspection of photographs. A substantial body of research has explored the effects of time limits on visual tasks, yet this investigation is the first to examine the impact of time constraints on both overall attention patterns and individual attention allocation at the fine spatial detail level. To this end, we conducted a series of experiments in which participants were asked to inspect black-and-white photographs within specified time constraints. Our findings indicate that the average attention directed toward shapes increased from approximately 60% without a time constraint to nearly 80% under time-constrained conditions, suggesting that the presence of time limitations indeed re-prioritize attention to shapes during visual inspection. Additionally, we discovered that the increased emphasis on shapes is not solely a result of participants rushing through their inspections, as this phenomenon persisted even after allowing for adequate time to process each image. These results have significant implications for the design of visual systems and decision-making protocols. The effectiveness of a filter relies on its ability to adapt to changing data patterns.  Traditional adaptive filters like dynamic and turbo filters utilize a fixed-sized bucket arrangement, which often results in inefficiencies when data distributions are dynamic.  To address this issue, we introduce the concept of support adaptivity, which leverages statistical characteristics of the data to optimize filter efficiency.  In this paper, we present the Cuckoo Filter, a dynamic filter that adapts to data patterns, and demonstrate its superiority over existing filters through both theoretical and experimental analysis.  The Cuckoo Filter outperforms the best existing filter in terms of space efficiency by 11-300%.  Furthermore, we extend our filter design to accommodate multi-precision data, developing the Adaptive Cuckoo Filter and achieving significant speedups of 4-80 over existing filters in query and deletion processes.  Our design is also optimized for hardware implementation, and experimental results confirm that it surpasses existing hardware filters in both efficiency and speed.  To our knowledge, this is the first adaptive filter to achieve such significant improvements.  An open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/ChenWZU/Cuckoo-Filter. The success of modern automation largely relies on the level of trust users have in it, which is influenced by factors such as the system's performance, control, and emotional connection. Although research has explored how trust develops over time, there is a lack of understanding on how trust evolves through continuous interactions between the user and the system. This study aims to bridge this gap by analyzing the impact of real-time system inputs and task outcomes on trust dynamics. A task requiring users to steer an aerial vehicle to target locations within a 3D environment was conducted, and the researchers examined the effects of varying levels of vehicle control, direction, and accuracy on trust development. Results showed that trust levels fluctuate rapidly following each interaction and stabilize in response to positive outcomes but decrease in response to negative outcomes. Notably, when the vehicle takes over control, trust levels increase significantly; however, when the user is in control, trust levels decrease. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating dynamic trust models into automation design to enhance performance and user trust. To enhance semi-supervised learning, particularly for imbalanced datasets, we propose an innovative approach called FlexMatch. FlexMatch consists of two primary components: Curriculum Pseudo Labeling and Consistency Regularization. The Curriculum Pseudo Labeling mechanism adjusts the soft labels based on a threshold to promote the model to focus on harder, easier, and unknown samples simultaneously. This adjustment leads to a more efficient learning process. We introduce TIPS, a novel method for generating high-resolution human images based on text descriptions and pose annotations. Unlike existing image creation techniques, TIPS utilizes a wide range of captions to inform both the pose and visual content of the generated image. This approach enables the reconstruction of both the subject's identity and physical appearance, resulting in highly realistic images. Through a combination of GAN and diffusion-based models, TIPS learns to capture the intricate details of the subject's face and clothing, while also incorporating the subject's pose from the provided annotation. This allows TIPS to create images with diverse poses and visual appearances, all from a single subject identity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TIPS on two datasets, pose2pose and DeepFashion, across a range of applications, including image creation, pose manipulation, and identity synthesis. Notably, TIPS's ability to generate images with a variety of poses and visual appearances, while maintaining subject identity, is a groundbreaking achievement in the field of human image creation. In this study, we examine a constrained Markov Decision Process, where rewards and penalties are intertwined within the same framework. A conventional approach to solving such problems involves formulating them as constrained Markov Decision Processes, where the goal is to maximize cumulative rewards subject to specific constraints. However, this method often results in complex problems due to the intricate interplay between rewards and penalties. To address this issue, we propose a novel policy gradient algorithm that decouples rewards from penalties, allowing for more manageable optimization. Our algorithm is founded on the principles of sequential minimization optimization, where constraints are progressively minimized to yield a globally convergent algorithm. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the algorithm converges at a linear rate under certain conditions, and we demonstrate its efficacy through simulated experiments. Our findings indicate that the algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency and convergence speed. Furthermore, we adapt this algorithm to tackle robust constrained Markov Decision Processes, where uncertainty in reward functions is accounted for by maximizing the minimum expected reward. Our approach is evaluated on a real-world inventory management scenario, where it successfully identifies optimal policies under various uncertainty conditions. The experimental results validate the algorithm's superiority over existing solutions in terms of both efficiency and convergence speed. We introduce SMURF, a novel approach for learning multi-frame optical flow that surpasses traditional methods by leveraging self-training and full-picture registration. Unlike prior approaches, SMURF eliminates the need for explicit motion prediction and warping modules, instead learning these skills from data through a self-learning process. The two-stage approach allows SMURF to learn a temporal filter that integrates these predictions, resulting in a more robust flow estimate. The filter's design is optimized for speed and accuracy, with SMURF outperforming leading competitors on various benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results. High-speed shadowgraphy has been employed to study the flow behavior in a low-density expansion tube's test section, characterized by a unique shape that combines a conical and cylindrical section, at Mach 0.7 and 1.5 flow speeds. This study aimed to investigate the formation of low-density regions, a phenomenon observed when a gas is rapidly cooled below its critical temperature, and examine how these regions develop at supersonic velocities. To achieve this, a specially designed expansion tube was used to generate flows with distinct velocity ratios, ranging from 2.5 to 4.0 times the speed of sound, at a low-pressure level of 0.37 bar. High-resolution shadowgraph images, captured at a rate of 1 kHz, revealed the complex flow behavior in the test section, and the resulting data were correlated with computational fluid dynamics simulations. The study demonstrated that CFD simulations accurately predicted the flow behavior, including the development of low-density regions, and the effects of boundary layer growth and shock wave interactions. However, CFD simulations failed to replicate the observed low-density regions, suggesting that the current numerical models are inadequate in predicting rarefied shock behavior. This discrepancy highlights the need for improved numerical models to accurately simulate low-density flow behavior. Additionally, this study provides valuable insights into the effects of rarefaction on shock dynamics, and the findings can be applied to the design of future hypersonic vehicles operating in the rarefied atmosphere of space. This study also contributes to the understanding of low-density flow behavior, a field that has been largely unexplored. A significant limitation of supervised learning is the substantial amount of labeled data required for effective model training. Active learning attempts to mitigate this issue by identifying a limited, representative set of unlabeled samples that can be effectively annotated. While most active learning methods focus on selecting samples with high uncertainty, this approach often results in poor test performance. This paper proposes a new active learning strategy that incorporates two key components: an enhanced test performance criterion and a uncertainty-based selection function. The former ensures model reliability, while the latter guides sampling. Experiments on image and text datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness, with superior test performance compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches. In machine learning, understanding the influence of reward on a model's behavior is crucial, especially when considering the potential for reward misspecification to lead to undesirable outcomes. This study examines the effects of reward misspecification on machine learning model performance in the context of behavior cloning, focusing on the outcomes in the driving domain. Our research reveals that the decision to include demographic information in the reward function can lead to significant performance disparities among various groups. Furthermore, we investigate the potential for reward misspecification to compromise model safety, specifically in relation to traffic sign detection, and propose a novel approach to mitigate this issue. Our proposed method, which involves incorporating the reward misspecification into a joint optimization framework with the model, can effectively mitigate sign detection disparities caused by demographic bias. This study highlights the need for a more in-depth understanding of reward misspecification and its implications on machine learning model behavior. Our findings emphasize the importance of reward design in ensuring the models produced by machine learning can be trusted and used responsibly. The rapid growth of IoT devices has led to a surge in data collection and processing, but it has also created a significant increase in computation-intensive tasks. To enhance the current state of computation offloading for IoT devices, this research proposes a novel self-serviced IoT architecture. Furthermore, a new computation offloading framework is presented, which enables users to have full control over offloading decisions. The results of experiments conducted on real-world devices demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed architecture and framework. Specifically, the experiments show that self-serviced IoT can reduce energy consumption by up to 92% and decrease latency by up to 60% in comparison to traditional cloud-based approaches. Moreover, the results indicate that the proposed self-serviced IoT architecture can handle a large number of tasks concurrently, outperforming traditional cloud-based approaches in terms of throughput. Additionally, the experiments demonstrate that the proposed computation offloading framework can reduce energy consumption by up to 40% compared to a traditional greedy approach. The research findings suggest that self-serviced IoT can be a promising solution for handling computation-intensive tasks in IoT devices. Future research directions include developing techniques to minimize the negative effects of self-serviced IoT on network traffic and developing methods to integrate self-serviced IoT with other emerging technologies like 5G and edge computing. We examine a paradox in quantum field theory where field operators, despite not being themselves entangled, can create and store entanglement between other systems. To resolve this, we investigate a simplified scenario involving a qubit coupled to a field operator and find that the operator's effect on entanglement depends on the direction of measurement relative to a specific basis. This leads to a clearer understanding of how the operator can facilitate entanglement swapping and how different measurement techniques can affect our perception of the operator's ability to store entanglement. Our analysis suggests that the ability of field operators to store entanglement is a result of entanglement swapping rather than the operators' inherent entanglement, and we propose further research into the impact of measurement techniques on quantum phenomena. This work draws on previous research by Braginsky, ITOP 2008, and Braginsky, Uhlmann, and Vuletic, Phys. Rev. A, 2009. This study examines the effectiveness of factor models in mortality prediction, specifically focusing on whether incorporating time-varying or time-invariant factors, as represented by dynamic principal component analysis (DPCA), yields superior results. We introduce an AMG coarsening method grounded in reinforcement learning that leverages an AmoebaNet-based initial setup for the state, coupled with a straightforward policy for iterative update. Our approach diverges from conventional rules that rely on the eigenvalue spectrum by allowing the system to converge concurrently with the top-left eigenvalue ratio. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves comparable performance to the industry-standard Cyclus AMG solver in three key areas: the cycle detection, stiffness classification, and overall solution accuracy. Notably, our technique boasts the added advantage of being fully automated, eliminating the need for human intervention in the coarsening process. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the system tends to favor the top-left eigenvalue ratio as the convergence stopping criterion, which aligns with the behavior of traditional AMG methods. This novel method's adaptability also extends to handling systems with variable conditioning, where it tends to focus on the stiffer components. Lastly, our study explores the potential to further enhance the solver's performance by incorporating additional updates to the state and policy, although the introduced modifications do not yield a significant improvement in the current implementation. We anticipate that this work will serve as a foundation for the development of more advanced reinforcement learning-based AMG methods in the future. In the field of Bayesian optimal control, achieving accurate policy search is a key challenge, particularly when relying on Monte Carlo estimates of the cost's gradient. These gradient estimates often come with significant uncertainty, but by leveraging this uncertainty, we can produce more reliable estimates through a process called sturdy sampling. Our research extends sturdy importance sampling to non-conjugate models and shows that it can be used to develop a more robust sampling method for Bayesian optimal transfer learning, leading to improved policy search results. Our experiments confirm that this method outperforms traditional importance sampling in reducing uncertainty and facilitating policy optimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be adapted to other gradient estimation techniques and applied to additional settings, such as multi-task learning. Our findings suggest that this method could lead to more reliable policy search results and efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs in complex reinforcement learning environments. A proposed method for analyzing censored data aims to determine the correlation between two continuous variables, accounting for instances where one variable is unmeasurable with uncertainty, based on a new unequal Tobit model. This approach involves three stages of computation to obtain the correlation coefficient, leveraging the asymptotic properties of sample moment estimates. A simulation study and real-world example are utilized to validate the method's effectiveness. Additionally, considering the substantial computational burden involved, a simplified version of the method is introduced to facilitate faster calculations. This simplified model employs a linear transformation to estimate the correlation coefficient directly, bypassing the initial estimation of key model parameters. A real-world application demonstrates the validity of this simplified method for censored data analysis. Finally, the method's robustness is compared to alternative correlation estimation techniques in a simulation study context. Determining the extent of sea ice in SAR imagery is crucial for both short-term weather forecasting and long-term climate analysis. However, accurately mapping ice boundaries is a complex task, particularly when dealing with diverse ice types that can create misleading appearances in SAR imagery. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages a U-Net architecture and utilizes a Bayesian framework to enhance the reliability of ice segmentation. By incorporating uncertainty estimates, our method can more effectively capture the nuances of ice boundaries and mitigate the effects of SAR imprints. Additionally, our approach allows for the transfer of knowledge between sequential SAR images and enables the evaluation of prediction uncertainty, making it a valuable tool for decision-making in applications like sea ice forecasting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a series of Arctic SAR images and comparing the results to those obtained by state-of-the-art alternatives. Our experiments reveal that our Bayesian U-Net model achieves superior performance in ice segmentation, particularly when evaluating the quality of segmentation and the associated prediction uncertainty. Our results are further validated by visual comparisons and quantitative metrics, including the Dice score and F1 score. These findings confirm that our method outperforms the baseline approaches in various ice conditions, emphasizing the importance of considering prediction uncertainty in SAR ice segmentation applications. Furthermore, real-time auction design is hindered by the vast number of auctions occurring daily on E-commerce platforms, along with the complexity of multiple variables involved, including item diversity, changing user preferences, and dynamic ad slots. To tackle these issues, a novel dynamic auction design is proposed for sponsored search on Lazada, an E-commerce platform with over 200,000 daily ads and 1,000 auctions per minute. By incorporating a sophisticated ranking system that incorporates both item content and past user behavior, along with a novel auction mechanism, our design achieves a revenue guarantee while also promoting high-quality ads. Experimental results demonstrate the success of this approach in enhancing the quality of ads without compromising revenue. Moreover, by incorporating a budget allocation system, our design is able to promote fair budget utilization among advertisers. This paper explores how to apply event structures to model and reason about programs using separate memory models, which focus on an abstract representation of program behavior. By utilizing these models, the research aims to establish a framework for analyzing programs that operate under separate memory through existing event structure theories. Initially, the concept of separate memory event structures is introduced, and its properties are identified. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that the developed framework can effectively capture data race conditions in programs using separate memory, and it achieves this through a case study of the C11 memory model, for which it was implemented in the Coq proof assistant. A new method has been proposed for enumerating general solution types of separable differential equations using HW hyper-Lambert maps. This approach involves transforming the equations into a known form, allowing for the application of established solution enumeration methods. A case study involving the HW-Lambert maps of the form y^(r-2)*(1+y)^m = Q(x,y) has been conducted, where Q is a rational function of a specific nature. This study has resulted in the derivation of enumeration formulas for equations with various rational and polynomial function relationships, expressed in terms of the Lambert W function. Furthermore, a connection between the HW-Lambert maps and other established transformation-based enumeration methods has been identified. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that the HW-Lambert maps can be viewed as a particular type of change of variables within the standard projective method for enumerating solutions. As a result, the standard projective method has been found to be a special instance of the HW-Lambert map enumeration method, with the projective method yielding solutions that are unique under specific conditions. Finally, this work has been extended to include the derivation of enumeration formulas for equations with arbitrary rational and polynomial function relationships, expressed in terms of the HW-Lambert maps. These formulas have been validated through numerical verification using multiple test cases. A software package implementing the HW-Lambert maps has been developed and made publicly available. This package has been shown to be a highly efficient tool for solving equations of this type, with the potential to be further extended to other types of equations. This work has been found to be a significant contribution to the field of separable equation solution enumeration. For example, it has been demonstrated that the HW-Lambert maps can be used to derive novel enumeration formulas for equations with the (r-2, m) parameters (2, 1) and (r, m) = (2, 2), which have not been previously reported in the literature. Smart buildings rely on smart metering infrastructure to monitor and track energy and environmental conditions, which has led to significant interest in using data from these systems to enhance customer comfort and reduce energy consumption.  However, the collection and dissemination of this data pose significant security risks, particularly in terms of protecting the privacy of users.  This issue is further complicated by the need to safeguard the integrity of metering data, prevent tampering and manipulation.  This paper introduces a novel security framework, called LiSA, which utilizes a lightweight and probabilistic approach to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and safety of metering data, and ensure seamless interoperability between various devices.  This framework incorporates a unique combination of techniques, including secure hardware elements, cryptographic processes, and zero-knowledge proofs to safeguard user privacy.  Furthermore, the proposed solution ensures compliance with relevant security standards and regulations, including NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 4 and NIST SP 800-121.  An example implementation of the LiSA framework is also presented, showcasing its key components and operational flow.  This paper concludes by highlighting the benefits of the LiSA framework and its potential to address the security challenges associated with smart metering infrastructure. Go's lightweight and primarily used for large-scale systems programming with concurrency, makes it a popular choice. However, Go's growing adoption also increases the likelihood of concurrency issues, making it essential to detect such problems. Existing methods, relying on source code analysis, may not be effective due to Go's binary-level language design and the challenges of converting source code into an executable form. This paper introduces BinGo, a binary-based concurrency bug detection tool, which leverages a combination of symbolic execution, dataflow analysis, and machine learning to identify concurrency bugs. By analyzing binary code, BinGo avoids source code conversion issues and improves performance, and its use of machine learning enables the incorporation of real-world data into the detection process. An evaluation of BinGo on 11 Go programs and 24 known concurrency bugs revealed its ability to identify 23 of these bugs, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, a comparison of BinGo with a source code analysis tool showed that it is significantly faster, with a time performance improvement of two orders of magnitude. The traditional knowledge distillation approach, which involves training a smaller model on a larger model's probability distributions, often proves difficult to implement in real-world scenarios due to its reliance on access to the larger model's parameters, which can be difficult to obtain. To address this limitation, we propose a novel knowledge distillation technique that leverages model checkpoints, which contain important information about a model's performance, and can be accessed without restriction. To capitalize on the benefits of model checkpoints, we develop a new knowledge distillation framework that incorporates two key components: an initial distillation phase, which utilizes the larger model's performance data to train a smaller model on a specific task, and a self-refinement phase, which utilizes the smaller model's performance data to further improve the smaller model's performance. To assess the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of our approach on a range of computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, and demonstrated its superiority over existing knowledge distillation methods. The results of our study indicate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three tasks, including a 2.2% improvement over existing knowledge distillation methods in image classification, a 0.4 point improvement in object detection, and a 0.3 point improvement in semantic segmentation. The implementation of our proposed method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChangWu1995/KD-from-Checkpoints.git. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly impacted the world and scientific research, 
with researchers across various disciplines working to comprehend the virus's 
biology and develop effective treatments. This study examines the pandemic's 
effect on scientific productivity in the life sciences by analyzing trends in 
publication numbers, author collaborations, and citation rates across different 
fields of study. The analysis reveals a significant surge in publications related 
to COVID-19, with notable increases in certain areas like computational biology 
and medicine. While some fields like microbiology and immunology initially saw a 
significant boost, others experienced a decline, such as a 30% reduction in 
genetics research. The findings suggest that the pandemic has accelerated the 
pace of scientific discovery, albeit with mixed effects on the quality of research. 
Moreover, the study highlights a rise in low-quality research, potentially due to 
the urgent need for new information on COVID-19. The analysis also indicates a 
prevalence of co-author collaborations among researchers studying COVID-19, with 
a notable increase in the number of co-authors per study. The results suggest that 
the pandemic has led to a shift towards specialization in certain areas while 
fostering a more interdisciplinary approach in others. The study's findings have 
important implications for understanding the pandemic's broader effects on 
scientific productivity. Ultimately, the research underscores the need for a more 
strategic approach to managing the pandemic's impact on research, such as adjusting 
publication and funding criteria to prioritize high-quality research. The study's 
results are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the pandemic's 
impact on research, with potential long-term benefits for the research community. 
This work is dedicated to the researchers who have dedicated their time and effort 
to studying COVID-19.

Call graph progression analysis involves extracting the evolution dynamics of software systems by studying changes in call graphs over time. This requires developing methods to accurately map call graphs to track function call relationships across different system versions. To address this challenge, we propose a three-step approach to construct call graphs for evolving systems. First, we identify all executable methods within each version of the software. Second, we use static program analysis to identify the relevant method call pairs. Lastly, we employ semantic method identification techniques to filter out non-relevant method call relationships. This approach enables us to develop a tool for analyzing call graphs of software systems. We have successfully applied our method to a series of versions of the Evolice Evolved Evolibrary Evolib software and found that the resulting call graphs can be used to reconstruct the evolution history of the system. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in accurately representing call graphs of evolving software systems. Furthermore, we propose using call graph progression analytics to extract valuable insights about the evolution dynamics of software systems. This includes identifying the most frequently called methods, analyzing the evolution of software components, and detecting performance issues such as performance bottlenecks and performance killers. Hyperspectral images are highly susceptible to noise from various sources, which severely impairs their quality. This noise not only diminishes the visual clarity of the images but also complicates their use in advanced applications. Conventional methods for removing noise from hyperspectral images often struggle to capture the intricate relationships between different spectral bands, which are crucial for achieving accurate results. In this study, a novel approach called SSCAN has been developed to address this challenge. SSCAN is an end-to-end model that utilizes a dual attention mechanism to automatically identify and eliminate noise from hyperspectral images. This attention mechanism enables the model to selectively focus on both the spatial and spectral characteristics of the images, thereby improving its ability to denoise them. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SSCAN in denoising hyperspectral images, with SSCAN outperforming existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Furthermore, SSCAN has been successfully applied to real-world hyperspectral images, with impressive results achieved on datasets such as VV and DW hyperspectral images. This study examines how the thermal equilibrium of Rayleigh-Benard convection behaves when the heat at the base is gradually increased, specifically up to 1000 times the ambient level. Building on previous research, we've developed a new approach that incorporates the effects of buoyancy into our analysis. This has led to a more accurate representation of the system, where the equilibrium temperature profile becomes steeper and more complex as the base heat flux increases. Our analysis also shows that the equilibrium state remains marginally stable, even in these conditions, and that the heat flux through the interface increases sublinearly with base heat flux. Notably, we've found that the system exhibits two distinct behaviors: for low base heat flux, the equilibrium is characterized by a cold, well-mixed layer, whereas for higher base heat flux, a boundary layer forms. Our results have implications for the stability of oceanic thermoclines, and we've also explored the application of our findings to other geophysical systems. Furthermore, we've identified areas for future research, including the study of the transient dynamics leading to these equilibrium states and the potential for turbulent behavior in these conditions. This work provides a new framework for understanding the dynamics of geophysical fluid dynamics, specifically in the study of oceanic thermoclines and oceanic heat transport. Ultimately, we believe that our results have the potential to significantly impact our understanding of ocean dynamics and climate modeling. A novel class of materials called spin-torque-induced ferrimagnets has been proposed to surpass traditional antiferromagnets by offering higher potential for ultra-fast magnetization reversal.  Specifically, half-metallic spin-torque-induced ferrimagnets, characterized by a significant disparity in the spin polarization of their ferromagnetic layers, have garnered attention for their rapid switching capabilities.  In this study, we employed first-principles calculations to investigate the potential of Mn$_2$RuGa as a prime candidate for a spin-torque-induced ferrimagnet, and we found that Mn$_2$RuGa indeed exhibits the required characteristics, including a substantial spin polarization in the majority channel, a significant difference in the spin polarization of its ferromagnetic layers, and a large spin-orbit coupling.  Our findings suggest that Mn$_2$RuGa is a suitable candidate for a spin-torque-induced ferrimagnet and we propose that its unique properties make it an ideal candidate for a highly efficient device capable of all-optical switching.  Moreover, we have identified a number of other potential candidates for spin-torque-induced ferrimagnets, including Mn$_2$CoGa, Mn$_2$CuGa, and Mn$_2$AgGa, and we have demonstrated that these materials have the required properties to function as spin-torque-induced ferrimagnets.  Our results provide a promising pathway for the development of highly efficient device capable of all-optical switching.  Importantly, our findings can be generalized to other materials with half-metallic properties, suggesting that Mn$_2$RuGa and its analogs are merely the initial discoveries in this rapidly growing field of research. A key factor in determining which elements are created is the stability of a specific type of nuclear reaction, particularly the instability resulting from the interaction of neighboring particles. To better understand this process, researchers have developed a method to quantify the stability of these interactions, taking into account the simultaneous influence of multiple particles. This approach involves modeling the evolution of these interactions over time and incorporating the effects of neighboring particles. This paper examines the challenge of estimating the state of a dynamic system, hidden from observation, through noisy and private channels controlled by an adversary. To mitigate the risk of system failure due to privacy breaches, eavesdropper interference must be limited. To achieve this goal, we formulate an optimization problem that balances system reliability and eavesdropper security, and show that this trade-off is optimal when a single solution exists. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of system parameters on the challenge of simultaneously ensuring privacy and reliability in this critical application. To address this issue, we introduce a new privacy-aware estimator that incorporates system parameters to guarantee both reliability and eprivacy, and our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in diverse system scenarios. To validate our findings, we test our proposed solution using a real-world example of a power system, and our results show significant improvements in eprivacy while maintaining reliable system performance. The findings of this research provide valuable insights for designing state estimators in various applications that require both reliability and eprivacy. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more trustworthy and secure state estimators for critical infrastructure applications. The adversarial robustness-accuracy tradeoff has been extensively studied in machine learning, yet its implications for robot learning remain unclear. This paper delves into the significance of this tradeoff in robot learning and presents a comprehensive overview of current research. We contend that adversarial samples can aid in the detection and mitigation of common robot failures, ultimately enhancing overall robot performance. We support this assertion by examining the effectiveness of adversarial samples in improving learning under common robot learning challenges, such as distribution shift, sensor noise, and out-of-distribution data. We also discuss the potential of adversarial training, a technique that can improve the adversarial robustness of robot learning systems. We believe that adversarial samples can play a pivotal role in robot learning, not solely as a means to achieve robustness but also as a tool to enhance overall robot performance. We hope that this review will stimulate further research on the utility of adversarial samples in robot learning and encourage the development of innovative applications. We also envision that this work will inspire researchers to explore the potential of adversarial training in robot learning and provide a foundation for future investigations into the connections between adversarial samples, robustness, and overall robot performance. This paper presents a groundbreaking approach to video comprehension through contrastive learning, enabling a visual encoder to distinguish between itself and a language encoder in a joint representation space. The task of open-set identification involves determining whether a given test sample originates from a known class set or not. This problem is particularly challenging when training and test samples come from different distributions. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative approach that utilizes sample augmentation to enhance the accuracy of OSI systems. Our method incorporates a similarity classifier that is trained alongside a primary classifier to identify in-class and out-of-class samples. By leveraging the augmented features from multiple iterations of feature extraction, we refine the similarity classifier's ability to distinguish similarities within and between classes. To further improve performance, we develop a similarity-based loss function that complements the classification loss for end-to-end training. Our experimental results on various benchmark datasets confirm the superiority of our augmentation-based method, yielding significant gains over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive ablation study to validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. The method, which is fully differentiable, can be easily integrated into existing deep learning architectures to enhance their open-set identification capabilities. Recent advancements in light field depth estimation have been hindered by the inherent occlusion problem, specifically when points in a scene create complex occlusions that have previously been addressed inadequately. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel method that leverages the inherent cross-ratios of occluded and non-occluded points within epipolar planes to construct a cost function. This cost function, in turn, enables the derivation of a cost map that distinguishes between occluded and non-occluded points. This cost map serves as a crucial input for our proposed CNN-based approach, which estimates depth by aggregating cross-ratio costs across all views. Our method's key benefits include its ability to handle complex occlusions effectively, its requirement for minimal training data, and the absence of the need for additional depth annotations during the training process. Our experiments conducted on real-world light field datasets have yielded promising results, demonstrating the superiority of our approach over existing methods in terms of depth accuracy, both quantitatively and qualitatively.
